content:
Heat and cold can both ease arthritis pain, but thin skin, numbness, diabetes or poor circulation make burns and cold injuries more likely, often without you feeling them happen. Heat usually suits stiffness and aching; cold usually suits a hot, swollen joint. Whichever you use, wrap the pack in a towel, keep sessions short, never sleep with it on, and look at your skin before and after. If you cannot feel hot and cold properly in that area, for example in numb feet from diabetes or nerve damage, do not use heat or ice there without checking with your GP, practice nurse or podiatrist first. Avoid cold packs on hands or feet affected by Raynaud's. Cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes and get help if it is large, deep or blistered. A single joint that is suddenly hot, swollen and very painful with fever needs same-day help, not a heat pack. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about using heat and cold safely when your skin or sensation is not what it was. For which one to choose for which kind of pain, see heat or ice for arthritis. For choosing and using heat packs, wheat bags and hot-water bottles, see heat packs: safe use.

Why thin skin, numbness and diabetes change the rules

The NHS says hot or cold packs can relieve osteoarthritis pain for some people, and NICE (NG226) lists them among things that can help alongside exercise. The risk is not the pack itself. It is skin that cannot warn you in time.

  • Thin skin comes with age, and also with long-term steroid tablets or strong steroid creams. It damages more easily and heals more slowly.
  • Numbness from nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy), often linked to diabetes, means you may not feel a burn or a cold injury happening. The NHS lists numbness, tingling and burning pain in the feet or hands as common symptoms.
  • Poor circulation means skin warms up and cools down unevenly and takes longer to recover. Raynaud's makes fingers and toes react badly to cold.
  • Tiredness, sleeping tablets or strong painkillers make it easier to doze off with a pack still on.

If any of these apply to you, the safest approach is gentle, short and checked.

Safe heat: a short checklist

  • Use warm, not hot. A hot-water bottle should be filled with hot tap water, not boiling water from the kettle, and have a cover.
  • Always put a towel or cover between the pack and your skin.
  • Keep sessions short, about 15 to 20 minutes, then take it off and let the skin rest.
  • Never sleep with a heat pack, wheat bag or hot-water bottle against you, and never sit or lie on one.
  • Heat microwave wheat bags exactly as the maker's instructions say. Overheated wheat bags can burn skin and have caused fires.
  • Do not use heat on top of a heat rub, a pain-relief gel or a patch unless your pharmacist says it is safe.
  • Do not use heat on skin that is broken, bruised, swollen and hot, or numb.

Warmth before gentle movement can make it easier to get going on a stiff morning. If cold weather is the main trigger, see cold weather and arthritis and keeping warm in a cold home.

Safe cold: a short checklist

  • Never put ice or a frozen pack straight on the skin. Wrap it in a damp tea towel.
  • Keep sessions short, about 10 to 15 minutes, and check the skin halfway through.
  • Stop if the skin goes white, blotchy, very red, numb or painful.
  • Avoid cold packs on hands or feet affected by Raynaud's, and on areas with poor circulation.
  • Cold usually suits a joint that is hot and swollen during a flare, but a flare that is new, unusual or not settling needs your GP or rheumatology advice line. See flare-ups.

If you have diabetes or numb feet

Feet are where things go wrong most often, because you cannot always see them and may not feel them. Do not put hot-water bottles, heat packs or ice on numb feet, and do not warm your feet by a fire or heater. Warm socks and bed socks are safer. Check your feet every day, or ask someone to check them, and tell your GP, practice nurse or podiatrist about any new blister, red patch, cut or colour change. For more on foot care, see diabetes, arthritis and your feet.

Check your skin before and after

Look at the skin before you start and when you finish. A little pinkness that fades quickly is normal. Stop using heat or cold on that area and ask for advice if you see:

  • blisters, broken skin or a red patch that does not fade;
  • a lacy, mottled brown or red rash where you often use heat, which can be a sign of too much heat too often;
  • skin that stays white, grey or numb after cold.

If you spend long periods sitting, look at skin and pressure care too.

If you get a burn

The NHS advice is to hold a burn or scald under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible. Do not use ice, creams or butter. Remove anything tight nearby unless it is stuck to the skin, then cover it loosely with cling film. Call 999 or go to A&E if the burn is large, deep, or the skin is white, charred or leathery. Contact NHS 111 if you are not sure what to do. Burns in people with diabetes or poor circulation can heal slowly, so tell your GP or practice nurse even about small ones.

Using heat packs safely

Heat packs and wheat bags can ease stiffness, but thin skin or reduced feeling can make burns more likely.

  • Follow the heating instructions exactly and do not overheat microwave packs.
  • Wrap the pack in a towel and check your skin every few minutes.
  • Do not lie on a heat pack or fall asleep with one.

When to get help

  • Same day: one joint is suddenly hot, swollen and very painful and you feel feverish or unwell. This can be a joint infection, and heat or ice will hide it rather than help. Contact your GP or NHS 111 the same day.
  • NHS 111 or your GP: a patch of skin becomes red, hot, swollen and spreading, which can be an infection such as cellulitis; or a burn or cold injury is not healing.
  • Call 999: a serious burn, or someone is very unwell and confused.
  • Routine GP or pharmacist: you are relying on heat or cold every day and pain is getting worse. Ask for a review of your pain plan and medicines. See the arthritis pain relief guide.

For family and carers

If the person you care for has diabetes, memory problems or numbness, check their skin after heat or cold, and make sure no pack goes to bed with them. Fill hot-water bottles for them if their hands are weak, and replace old or perished ones.

Common questions

Is heat or ice better for arthritis?

Many people find heat better for stiffness and aching, and cold better for a hot, swollen joint. Try what suits you, carefully. The full comparison is in heat or ice for arthritis.

Can I use a heat pack if I have diabetes?

Not on numb areas, especially feet. If you have normal feeling in that area, use it warm rather than hot, wrapped, for a short time, and check your skin afterwards. Ask your diabetes team or podiatrist if you are unsure.

Can I use an electric blanket?

Use it to warm the bed and switch it off before you get in, unless it is designed to stay on overnight. Check it is in good condition. People with numbness should ask their GP or nurse first.
